4. Types of Disk Scheduling Algorithms
5.1 FCFS (First Come First Serve)
FCFS serves the disk requests in the order they arrive. It is simple but may
result in long waiting times when requests are far apart on the disk surface.
5.2 SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First)
SSTF selects the request closest to the current head position. It reduces
seek time but can cause starvation for distant requests.
5.3 SCAN (Elevator Algorithm)
In SCAN, the disk arm moves in one direction serving requests until it
reaches the end, then reverses direction. It behaves like an elevator moving
up and down, hence the name.
5.4 C-SCAN (Circular SCAN)
C-SCAN moves the head in one direction only. After reaching the end, it
quickly returns to the beginning without serving any requests. It provides
uniform wait time compared to SCAN.
5.5 LOOK
LOOK works like SCAN but instead of going till the end of the disk, it
reverses direction when there are no more requests ahead.
5.6 C-LOOK
C-LOOK is a modified version of C-SCAN that only goes as far as the last
request in each direction, then jumps back to the first request.

9. Conclusion
Disk scheduling is a crucial part of operating systemdesign that directly
impacts the speed and efficiency of data access. Since a disk drive handles
multiple read and write requests from different processes at the same
time, it becomes essential to determine the most efficient order in which
these requests are executed. Proper disk scheduling reduces seek time,
response time, and rotational delay, leading to faster data retrieval and
improved system performance.
Various disk scheduling algorithms like FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK,
and C-LOOK are designed to optimize performance based on different
situations. Each has its own advantages and limitations, but their common
goal is to minimize disk head movement and maximize throughput.
In modern systems such as servers, databases, and cloud storage, disk
scheduling ensures that multiple users and processes can access data
efficiently without long waiting times. It not only improves hardware
utilization but also enhances the overall reliability and speed of the
computer system.
In conclusion, disk scheduling is essential for achieving balanced, fair, and
high-performance data access, making it a fundamental aspect of every
operating system’s resource management.
